gloss: mount and ride; make ride; chariot, chariotry; rider; upper millstone
summary: To mount and be upon a beast or a vehicle, and so to ride: on a donkey, mule, camel or horse, or in a chariot. The qal rides, and its participle רֹכֵב is the rider, above all in “horse and its rider” (Exo 15:1); the hiphil sets someone on a mount or in a chariot, as Joseph in Pharaoh's second chariot and Solomon on David's mule. The nouns are what is ridden: רֶכֶב the chariot and a king's whole chariotry, מֶרְכָּבָה the chariot, and רֶכֶב also the upper millstone that rides on the lower. Yahweh “rides the heavens” and the cloud (Deu 33:26; Isa 19:1), his chariots are fire and whirlwind (2Ki 6:17; Isa 66:15), and Israel is told to trust not in chariots but in his name (Psa 20:8), while her king comes “riding on a donkey” (Zec 9:9; Mat 21:5). Arabic rakiba, Akkadian rakābu, Ugaritic and Sabaean rkb all “ride, mount”, and Akkadian narkabtu “chariot” and narkabu “upper grindstone” match the Hebrew nouns.

words.gloss: chariotry, chariots; a chariot; riders; upper millstone
words.summary: About 120 times. Mostly collective: the chariot force of Egypt, Canaan, Aram, Israel and the nations, counted in hundreds and thousands and named beside horses and horsemen (פָּרָשִׁים). It is also one king's own chariot, a company of riders (Isa 21:7, 9), and, three times, the upper millstone, the stone that rides on the lower (Deu 24:6; Jdg 9:53; 2Sa 11:21), as Akkadian narkabu is the upper grindstone beside narkabtu the chariot.

senses.definition: A force of war chariots, counted by number and set beside horses and horsemen; the strength of Egypt and of the kings of the land, and a thing men trust in.

evidence.note: “He took six hundred chosen רֶכֶב, and all the רֶכֶב of Egypt, and officers over all of it.”
The waters covered “the chariots and the horsemen, all the army of Pharaoh”.
“The horse of Pharaoh went with his chariotry (בְּרִכְבּוֹ) and his horsemen into the sea.”
“All the Canaanites who dwell in the valley have רֶכֶב בַּרְזֶל.”
Judah could not drive out those of the valley “because they had chariots of iron”.
Jabin had “nine hundred chariots of iron” and oppressed Israel twenty years.
“Solomon gathered רֶכֶב and horsemen; he had 1,400 רֶכֶב and 12,000 horsemen, and he put them in the cities of the chariotry (עָרֵי הָרֶכֶב).”
David hamstrung “all the chariot horses (הָרֶכֶב), but left of them a hundred”.
“When you see horse and chariot (סוּס וָרֶכֶב), a people greater than you, do not fear them, for Yahweh your God is with you.”
“These in chariots and these in horses, but we will remember the name of Yahweh our God.”
Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help “and trust in chariots because they are many”.
“At your rebuke, God of Jacob, both chariot and horse lay stunned.”
Yahweh “who brings out chariot and horse, army and strength; they lie down together, they shall not rise”.
“I will cut off רֶכֶב from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem … and he shall speak peace to the nations.”
The king of the north comes against him “with chariots and horsemen and many ships”.

senses.definition: A single chariot, a king's or a commander's, harnessed, ridden and fought from.

evidence.note: “Jehoram said, Harness (אֱסֹר); and he harnessed his chariot (רִכְבּוֹ), and they went out, each in his chariot.”
Jehoram, shot between the arms, “sank down in his chariot”.
Ahab “was propped up in the chariot (בַּמֶּרְכָּבָה) … and the blood of the wound ran into the bottom of the chariot (הָרָכֶב)”: the two nouns of one chariot.
Jehu's men “made him ride in his chariot”.
Josiah's servants took him from the chariot (הַמֶּרְכָּבָה) and set him “on his second chariot (רֶכֶב הַמִּשְׁנֶה)”.
“Kings and princes sitting on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses.”

senses.definition: Those who ride, as a body: a troop seen coming on donkeys, camels or horses.

evidence.note: “When he sees רֶכֶב, pairs of horsemen, רֶכֶב of donkeys, רֶכֶב of camels”: a riding company, named by what it rides.
“Behold, here comes רֶכֶב אִישׁ, pairs of horsemen; and he answered, Fallen, fallen is Babylon.”
“You shall be filled at my table with horse and רֶכֶב, mighty man and every man of war”: beside the warriors, the riders.

senses.gloss: chariots of fire; the chariotry of God
senses.definition: Yahweh's own chariotry: the chariot of fire that parted Elijah and Elisha, the fiery horses and chariots round Elisha, the myriads of Psa 68; and the prophet called “the chariotry of Israel”, its real defence.

evidence.note: “Behold, רֶכֶב־אֵשׁ and horses of fire, and they parted the two of them, and Elijah went up in the whirlwind to the heavens.”
Yahweh opened the young man's eyes, “and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha”.
“The chariotry of God (רֶכֶב אֱלֹהִים) is twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them, Sinai in holiness.”
Elisha cried, “My father, my father, רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו!”
Joash weeps over the dying Elisha with the same words: the prophet was Israel's chariotry and horsemen.
“The Lord had made the army of Aram hear the sound of chariotry, the sound of horses, the sound of a great army.”

senses.definition: The upper stone of a hand mill, which rides on the lower (רֵחַיִם); a slab of it is heavy enough to kill.

evidence.note: “No one shall take the mill (רֵחַיִם) or the upper stone (וָרָכֶב) in pledge, for he would be taking a life (נֶפֶשׁ) in pledge”: the household's daily bread.
“A woman threw פֶּלַח רֶכֶב on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.”
Joab recalls it: “Did not a woman throw on him פֶּלַח רֶכֶב from the wall?”

evidence.locator: Exo.14.7, 28; Psa.20.8; Zec.9.10, רֶכֶב → ἅρμα; ἅρμα renders רֶכֶב ×83

evidence.note: “The sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots (ἁρμάτων) of many horses running to battle”, after Jol 2:4–5.
The Ethiopian eunuch “sitting in his chariot (ἅρματος) reading the prophet Isaiah”.

evidence.locator: 2Sa.11.21, רֶכֶב → μύλου; Deu.24.6 → ἐπιμύλιον; Jdg.9.53 → ἐπιμυλίου

evidence.note: “A mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone (μύλον) and threw it into the sea, saying, So shall Babylon be thrown down.”

parallels.note: “Horseman”: chariots and horsemen, the two arms of a mounted force.
“Horse”: horse and chariot, the strength men trust instead of Yahweh.

opposites.note: “The name of Yahweh”: what Israel remembers and boasts in, against the nations' chariots.

phrases.gloss: the chariotry of Israel and its horsemen (of a prophet)

words.gloss: mount, ride; (hiphil) make ride, set upon
words.summary: About eighty times. The core is being upon what carries one: mounting a beast and riding it, or riding in a chariot; the hiphil puts someone or something upon it. Arabic rakiba is defined the same way, “be upon, get upon”, and is used of riding a beast and boarding a ship.

stems.gloss: mount, ride; (participle) rider; (of God) ride the heavens, the cloud, a cherub

senses.definition: To get up on a donkey, mule, camel or horse and go on it.

evidence.note: “Rebekah and her maids arose, וַתִּרְכַּבְנָה on the camels, and went after the man.”
“Saddle the donkey for me; and they saddled the donkey for him, and he rode on it.”
Mephibosheth: “I will saddle the donkey and ride on it and go with the king, for your servant is lame.”
Balaam “was riding on his donkey”.
“Am I not your donkey on which you have ridden all your life to this day?”
Jair “had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys”: the mark of rank.
“You who ride on white donkeys, who sit on rich carpets.”
Abigail “riding on the donkey and coming down under cover of the mountain”.
None escaped “except four hundred young men who rode on camels and fled”.
The king's sons “each mounted his mule and fled”.
“Absalom was riding on the mule … and the mule that was under him went on.”
The Shunammite to her servant: “Drive on; do not slow the riding for me.”
“No beast was with me except the beast I rode on.”
“A horse that the king has ridden on.”
“Any saddle (הַמֶּרְכָּב) on which he who has a discharge rides shall be unclean.”
“A man riding on a red horse, standing among the myrtles.”
“Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saved, humble, וְרֹכֵב עַל־חֲמוֹר, on a colt the foal of she-donkeys.”
Zec 9:9 fulfilled as Jesus enters Jerusalem: “mounted (ἐπιβεβηκώς) on a donkey”; the Peshitta has וַרכִֿיבֿ, the root's participle.
“Behold, your king comes, sitting on a donkey's colt”; Peshitta וַרכִֿיבֿ.

senses.definition: To mount a chariot and drive in it.

evidence.note: As the rain came, “Ahab rode (וַיִּרְכַּב) and went to Jezreel”, having harnessed his chariot (1Ki 18:44).
“Jehu rode and went to Jezreel”, driving furiously (2Ki 9:20).
“You and I were riding in pairs behind Ahab his father.”
Kings and princes “riding in chariots and on horses”.

senses.definition: רֹכֵב as a noun: the one on the horse, above all in war, named with the horse he rides and falling with it.

evidence.note: “Horse and its rider (סוּס וְרֹכְבוֹ) he has thrown into the sea.”
Dan a serpent “that bites the horse's heels, so that its rider falls backward”.
“The rider of the horse shall not save his life.”
Jehoram sent “a rider on a horse” to meet Jehu.
Rabshakeh: “I will give you two thousand horses, if you can put riders on them.”
Of Yahweh's war club: “with you I shatter horse and its rider, with you I shatter chariot and its rider.”
“I will overthrow the chariot and its riders, and the horses and their riders shall go down, each by the sword of his brother.”
“I will strike every horse with panic and its rider with madness.”
Judah's men “shall fight, for Yahweh is with them, and the riders on horses shall be put to shame”.
Assyria's young men, “horsemen riding on horses”.
Gog comes “from the uttermost parts of the north, you and many peoples with you, all of them riding on horses”.
The ostrich “laughs at the horse and its rider”.
Couriers “riding on swift horses used in the king's service”.

senses.gloss: (of God) ride the heavens, the cloud, a cherub
senses.definition: Yahweh pictured as a rider coming swiftly to help his people or to judge: on the heavens, on a swift cloud, on a cherub, on his horses and chariots.

evidence.note: “There is none like God, Jeshurun, רֹכֵב שָׁמַיִם to your help, and in his majesty on the skies.”
“He rode on a cherub and flew; he soared on the wings of the wind” (2Sa 22:11).
“Behold, Yahweh rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt, and the idols of Egypt tremble before him.”
“Lift up a song to him who rides through the desert plains (בָּעֲרָבוֹת); Yah is his name.”
“To him who rides in the heavens of heavens of old.”
“Was your wrath against the sea, that you rode on your horses, your chariots of salvation?”

senses.gloss: ride on (for a cause); ride (as trust)
senses.definition: Riding as going out in power: the king riding on for truth, and Israel's resolve to ride on horses, that is, to trust in them, and its renouncing of it.

evidence.note: “In your majesty prosper, רְכַב, for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness.”
“You said, No, we will flee on horses … and, We will ride on swift ones (עַל־קַל נִרְכָּב); therefore your pursuers shall be swift.”
“Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses, and we will say no more, Our God, to the work of our hands.”

stems.gloss: make ride, set on a mount or in a chariot; set upon; put (the hand) on; harness

senses.gloss: make ride, set (someone) on a mount or in a chariot
senses.definition: To put a person on a beast or in a chariot: in honour, as a king or a favourite is set on the king's own mount; for a journey; or the wounded and the dead carried home.

evidence.note: Pharaoh “made him ride (וַיַּרְכֵּב) in his second chariot, and they cried before him, Abrek, and set him over all the land of Egypt”.
David: “Make Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon”, there to be anointed king.
“Let them make him ride on the horse through the city square, and proclaim, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honour.”
“Moses took his wife and his sons and set them on the donkey.”
Ahaziah's servants “carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem” and buried him.
Josiah's servants “carried him dead in a chariot from Megiddo”.
“They threw their garments on the colt and set Jesus on it (ἐπεβίβασαν)”; the Peshitta uses the root's causative, וַארכּבֻֿוה_י.

senses.definition: To set a thing on what carries it: the ark on a cart, a man on the wind; and, as Yahweh's gift, to set his people high upon the land.

evidence.note: “They set the ark of God on a new cart and carried it from the house of Abinadab.”
“He made him ride on the high places of the earth, and he ate the produce of the field.”
“Then you shall delight yourself in Yahweh, and I will make you ride on the high places of the earth, and feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father.”
“You made men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water, yet you brought us out to abundance.”
“You lift me up on the wind, you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the storm.”

senses.definition: To lay the hand on the bow, ready to draw.

evidence.note: Elisha to the king of Israel: “הַרְכֵּב יָדְךָ עַל־הַקֶּשֶׁת; and he put his hand on it, and Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands.”

senses.definition: To put a draught animal under the yoke and set a rider or driver on it for heavy work.

evidence.note: “Ephraim was a trained heifer that loved to thresh … אַרְכִּיב אֶפְרַיִם; Judah shall plough, Jacob shall harrow for himself.”

evidence.locator: Zec.9.9, רֹכֵב → ἐπιβεβηκὼς; Psa.18.11; 1Ki.13.13; 1Sa.25.42; Zec.1.8; ἐπιβαίνω renders רָכַב ×6, and the participle ἐπιβεβηκότες ×4 more

evidence.note: Zec 9:9 quoted: “your king comes to you, humble, and mounted (ἐπιβεβηκώς) on a donkey.”
“Finding a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went on board (ἐπιβάντες)”: the same mounting of a ship as Arabic rakiba.

evidence.locator: 2Ki.9.28; 23.30, hiphil of רָכַב → ἐπιβιβάζω ×2

evidence.note: “They set Jesus on it (ἐπεβίβασαν)”, as Solomon was set on David's mule (1Ki 1:33).
The Samaritan “set him on his own beast (ἐπιβιβάσας)”.
“Provide mounts, that they may set Paul on them (ἐπιβιβάσαντες)”; the Peshitta has דּנַרכּבֻֿונ.

parallels.note: “Fly”: Yahweh rides on a cherub and flies.
“Flee”: we will flee on horses, we will ride on swift ones.
“Saddle”: the donkey is saddled, then ridden.

phrases.gloss: make ride on the high places of the earth

words.summary: About forty-five times: the chariot, singly or in the plural, of kings, of war, and once the pattern of the cherubim of the ark called “the chariot” (1Ch 28:18). It does not differ in sense from רֶכֶב, which the same verses use beside it (1Ki 22:35; 2Ch 35:24); it is the form the other languages share, Akkadian narkabtu, Ugaritic mrkbt, Syriac markabtā, and Egyptian borrowed it as mrkbt.

senses.definition: A wheeled chariot drawn by horses: for a ruler's state, for travel and for war.

evidence.note: Joseph is made to ride “בְּמִרְכֶּבֶת הַמִּשְׁנֶה”, Pharaoh's second chariot.
“Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father.”
The stands' wheels were made “like the work of a chariot wheel (אוֹפַן הַמֶּרְכָּבָה)”.
Yahweh “took off the wheels of their chariots, so that they drove heavily”.
“Pharaoh's chariots and his army he cast into the sea.”
“You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.”
The way of the king: “he will take your sons and set them for himself in his chariots … and they shall run before his chariots.”
“Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.”
Rehoboam “made haste to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem”.
Ahab “took him up into the chariot”.
Naaman “came down from the chariot to meet him”.
Jehu took Jehonadab son of Rechab “up to him into the chariot”.
“Their land is full of horses, and there is no end to their chariots.”
“I will cut off your horses from among you and destroy your chariots.”
“I will overthrow the chariot and its riders (מֶרְכָּבָה וְרֹכְבֶיהָ)”: the chariot and the verb's participle together.
“The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot.”
The locust army: “like the sound of chariots on the tops of the mountains they leap.”
The locusts of the fifth trumpet: “the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots”; Peshitta דּמַרכּבָֿתָֿא.
Josiah “burned the chariots of the sun with fire”.
Shebna: “there you shall die, and there the chariots of your glory”.

senses.gloss: the chariots of Yahweh; the chariot of the cherubim
senses.definition: Yahweh's chariots, of fire and whirlwind, in which he comes to judge or to save; and the gold cherubim over the ark, called “the chariot”.

evidence.note: “Behold, Yahweh will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury and his rebuke in flames of fire.”
“You rode on your horses, מַרְכְּבֹתֶיךָ יְשׁוּעָה.”
The gold “for the pattern of the chariot (הַמֶּרְכָּבָה), the cherubim that spread their wings and cover the ark of the covenant of Yahweh”.
Of the destroyer from the north: “his chariots like the whirlwind”, the figure turned against Judah.
“Four chariots coming out from between two mountains of bronze”, which are “the four spirits of the heavens, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth” (Zec 6:5).

evidence.locator: Gen.41.43; Exo.15.4; Isa.66.15, מֶרְכָּבָה → ἅρμα; ἅρμα renders מֶרְכָּבָה ×31

evidence.note: “Go near and join this chariot (ἅρματι)”; Peshitta למַרכַּבֿתָֿא.
“He commanded the chariot to stand still.”
Among Babylon's merchandise, “horses and chariots (ῥεδῶν) and bodies and souls of men”; the Peshitta's word is ומַרכּבָֿתָֿא.

words.summary: Three times: the man who drives a king's chariot, and a mounted messenger. The form names one whose trade is riding.

senses.definition: The one who drives the chariot while the king fights from it; and a rider sent with a message.

evidence.note: The wounded king “said to his charioteer (לְרַכָּבוֹ), Turn your hand and carry me out of the battle”.
“Take a horseman (רַכָּב) and send him to meet them”; he goes “on horseback” (2Ki 9:18, רֹכֵב הַסּוּס).

words.summary: Three times: what one rides on or in, a saddle, the seat of Solomon's litter, and collectively the chariots of Solomon. Arabic markab, “anything upon which one rides”, is the same formation.

senses.definition: The seat or saddle on which one rides.

evidence.note: “Any מֶרְכָּב on which he who has a discharge rides (יִרְכַּב) shall be unclean.”
Of Solomon's litter: “its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat (מֶרְכָּבוֹ) of purple”.

senses.definition: Chariots collectively, as רֶכֶב.

evidence.note: “Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots (לְמֶרְכָּבוֹ), and twelve thousand horsemen.”

words.summary: Once, the act of riding, in Tyre's trade.

senses.definition: Riding; saddle-cloths are “garments of spreading for riding”.

evidence.note: “Dedan traded with you in saddle-cloths (בִגְדֵי־חֹפֶשׁ) for riding (לְרִכְבָּה).”

words.summary: Once, of the clouds as Yahweh's vehicle. Akkadian rukūbu “vehicle, mount, boat” is the same formation.

senses.definition: That on which one rides; the clouds made Yahweh's chariot.

evidence.note: “Who makes the clouds his chariot (רְכוּבוֹ), who walks on the wings of the wind.”

words.gloss: ride; (aphel) set on a mount; (ethpaal) be fitted together
words.summary: The Peshitta's verb of the root: to ride, of the colt no one had ridden and of the king of Zec 9:9; its causative, to set Jesus and Paul on a mount; and, in Paul's letters, the passive of the doubled stem for the body and the building “fitted together”. That last sense is Arabic rakkaba “set one part upon another, compose”: what is set upon another is joined to it.

senses.definition: To ride on a beast.

evidence.note: Zec 9:9: “your king comes to you, humble, וַרכִֿיבֿ עַל חמָרָא.”
“Your king comes to you, וַרכִֿיבֿ on a colt, the foal of a she-donkey.”
“A colt tied, on which no one of men has ridden (לָא רַכֿבֵּה).”
“… on which no man has ever ridden (לָא רכֵֿבֿ).”

senses.definition: To make someone ride, setting him on the beast.

evidence.note: “They put their garments on the colt וַארכּבֻֿוה_י ליֵשֻוע on it.”
“Prepare a beast, that they may set Paul on it (דּנַרכּבֻֿונ לפַּולָוס) and bring him safe to Felix.”

senses.definition: Of the building and the body of believers in Christ: to be joined part to part into one whole.

evidence.note: “In him the whole building מֵתֿרַכַּבֿ and grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (συναρμολογουμένη).
“From him the whole body מֵתֿרַכַּבֿ וּמֵתֿקַטַר by every joint”: fitted and knit together.
The head, “from whom the whole body מֵתֿרַכַּבֿ and is held together by joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God”.

words.summary: The Peshitta's chariot, the Hebrew מֶרְכָּבָה, for ἅρμα and ῥέδη.

senses.definition: A chariot, for travel or war.

evidence.note: The eunuch “was sitting in the chariot (עַל מַרכַּבֿתָֿא) and reading Isaiah the prophet”.
“He commanded the chariot to stand.”
“Like the sound of chariots of many horses running to battle.”

words.summary: Once in the Peshitta, for ζευκτηρία, the lashings that hold a ship's steering oars. Like the ethpaal “be fitted together”, it is what joins one thing to another; its tie to riding runs through that sense, as Arabic rakkaba “set one part on another, fix”.

senses.definition: A band that fastens one part to another.

evidence.note: “They loosed רָכֿבֵּא דּסַוכָּנֵא”: the fastenings of the rudders.

cognates.gloss: be upon, get upon; mount and ride (a beast); embark in (a ship)
cognates.note: Defined as عَلَا “be upon, get upon”, of which riding a beast and boarding a ship are uses: the same core as the Hebrew, where the hiphil sets a man or the ark upon what carries it.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1142, art. ركب, رَكِبَهُ (n16451)
evidence.note: “I. q. عَلَاهُ … I rode, or rode upon, and I mounted, or mounted upon, the beast … I embarked in the ship … It was, or became, upon, or over, it; got upon it.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1142, art. ركب, اركب (n16453)
evidence.note: Form IV: “He gave him … an animal on which to ride … He mounted me, or made me to ride, behind him”: the hiphil.

evidence.locator: SEM000360 rkb [ride] V, ARB011434 rakiba [Mounted]

cognates.note: The rider, and a body of riders, as רֹכֵב, רַכָּב and the collective רֶכֶב of Isa 21:7, 9.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1144, art. ركب, رَاكِبٌ (n16475)

doctrine.statement: When David's son was to be made king, David commanded, “make Solomon my son ride (וְהִרְכַּבְתֶּם) on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon”, where he was anointed and the people cried “Let king Solomon live” (1Ki 1:33–39); judges' sons rode on donkeys (Jdg 10:4; 12:14). Zechariah foretells: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion … behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saved, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt the foal of she-donkeys”, and goes straight on, “I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations, and his dominion shall be from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth” (Zec 9:9–10). The gospels say Jesus fulfilled the first part: the disciples “set Jesus on” the colt, and the crowd cried, “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord” (Luk 19:35–38; Mat 21:5; Jhn 12:15). From the verses: Jesus came to Jerusalem as the son of David set on his mount to be king, humble and not in a chariot; the dominion from sea to sea that follows in the same prophecy, with the chariot and the war horse cut off, is the kingdom he will reign over on the earth.

Israel's king was not to multiply horses or to send the people back to Egypt for them (Deu 17:16), and Israel was told, “when you see horse and chariot, a people greater than you, do not fear them, for Yahweh your God is with you” (Deu 20:1). Pharaoh's chariots and their riders went down in the sea (Exo 14:28; 15:1, 4, 19); Joshua was told to burn the Canaanites' chariots (Jos 11:6); and the psalm says, “these in chariots and these in horses, but we will remember the name of Yahweh our God” (Psa 20:8). Isaiah's woe is on those who “trust in chariots because they are many … but do not look to the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 31:1), and in Hosea Israel's repentance is to say, “Assyria shall not save us, we will not ride on horses” (Hos 14:4). Yahweh will cut off Judah's own horses and chariots in that day (Mic 5:9), and overthrow “the chariot and its riders” of the kingdoms of the nations (Hag 2:22). From the verses: chariots stand for the strength men trust instead of God, and he breaks that strength, his people's and the nations', so that their trust is in him alone.

Yahweh is “the rider of the heavens” who comes to Israel's help (Deu 33:26); he “rode on a cherub and flew” to deliver David (Psa 18:11); he “rides on a swift cloud” to judge Egypt (Isa 19:1) and makes “the clouds his chariot” (Psa 104:3), where the next verse says he makes his messengers spirits (or winds) and his ministers a flaming fire (Psa 104:4), a verse applied to the angels, “ministering spirits sent out to serve” (Heb 1:7, 14). His chariotry is “twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them, Sinai in holiness” (Psa 68:18), the myriads with whom he came at Sinai (Deu 33:2). When Elisha's servant feared the army of Aram, Yahweh opened his eyes and “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha” (2Ki 6:16–17); the four chariots of Zechariah are “the four spirits of the heavens, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth” (Zec 6:1–5). Isaiah foretells, “Yahweh will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury” (Isa 66:15), and Paul says the Lord Jesus will be “revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, rendering vengeance” (2Th 1:7–8). From the verses: God's chariots are his angels and his power at work in the world, by which he guards his servants, and with them Christ will come to judge at his return.

As Elijah and Elisha walked, “behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire, and they parted the two of them, and Elijah went up in the whirlwind (בַּסְעָרָה) to the heavens (הַשָּׁמָיִם)” (2Ki 2:11): the chariot parted them, and it was the whirlwind that took him up into the sky, the heavens where the birds fly (Gen 1:20). The sons of the prophets supposed “the spirit of Yahweh has taken him up and cast him on some mountain or into some valley” (2Ki 2:16). Afterwards a letter came “from Elijah the prophet” to Jehoram king of Judah, foretelling his sickness (2Ch 21:12–15). Jesus said, “no one has ascended into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of man” (Jhn 3:13); of the faithful of old, “these all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13, 39–40). From the verses: Elijah was carried away by Yahweh's power and did not go to dwell with God in heaven; like the rest of the faithful he waits for the resurrection to receive the promise.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key רכב; no existing entry used it. BDB keys: t.cq.aa verb, t.cq.ab רֶכֶב, t.cq.ac רִכְבָּה, t.cq.ad רַכָּב, t.cq.ae רְכוּב, t.cq.ah מֶרְכָּב, t.cq.ai מֶרְכָּבָה; the name Rechab (t.cq.af) and the gentilic Rechabite (t.cq.ag) in names/rechab.json. Left unassigned: t.cq.aj רֵכָה Recah, a place (1Ch 4:12; TIPNR has Recah@1Ch.4.12 as a place, not a person), whose spelling has no ב and may not be of this root; the brief's five tokens for it and for t.cq.ag are the same shared spellings (the four הָרֵכָבִים of Jer 35 are the gentilic); m.dm.ak, a zero-token cross-reference. Beth-marcaboth (בֵּית מַרְכָּבוֹת, Jos 19:5; 1Ch 4:31, “house of chariots”, BDB b.bp.bg) is a place name and is not drafted; one of its tokens is counted under מֶרְכָּבָה by spelling. The Aramaic אַרְכֻבָּה “knee” (Dan 5:6) stays in barak, where it already is; Arabic rukba “knee” is filed under rkb in Lane (p. 1143, n16460), so whether knee belongs to this root or to ברך is open. No Biblical Aramaic word of the root. Greek: no loans; ἅρμα, μύλος, ἐπιβαίνω and ἐπιβιβάζω are renderings only. Rev 18:13's Greek is ῥέδη, not ἅρμα; it is cited for the Peshitta's word. Doctrine: Deu 17:16 (horses, not this root) and Deu 33:2, Psa 104:4, Heb 1:7, 14, 2Th 1:7–8 are cited for context; Elijah's letter (2Ch 21:12) is read as written after his taking up, since Elisha was already serving in Jehoshaphat's reign (2Ki 3:11) — a chronological argument to review. Leads not followed: Ugaritic rkb ʿrpt “rider of the clouds”, Baal's epithet, compared with Psa 68:5 and Deu 33:26 (DULAT not vendored; not recorded); Ge'ez ረከበ in Dillmann (sense unverified, so marked possible); Payne Smith for ܪܟܒ beyond SEDRA; Sabaean in Biella/SabaWeb. Open questions: (1) whether רֶכֶב at Ezk 39:20 is “rider” or “chariot”; (2) whether the millstone sense is “the rider stone” or a separate word, as Akkadian keeps narkabu and narkabtu apart; (3) the doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
